\chapter*{The Malayalam script --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Malayalam script (reference)}
\markboth{Malayalam script}{Malayalam script}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — a place to look things up. You are \emph{not} meant to read this before the lessons: the lessons teach reading through real words, introducing each letter as a word needs it. This page just gathers the system in one spot.

\section*{How the Malayalam script works (the three facts the lessons teach)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \ml{ക} = \textquotedblleft{}ka,\textquotedblright{} \ml{മ} = \textquotedblleft{}ma,\textquotedblright{} \ml{ര} = \textquotedblleft{}ra.\textquotedblright{} You never write the short \emph{a} — it's already there.
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign changes that built-in vowel.} Attached to a consonant it gives \ml{കാ} = kā · \ml{കി} = ki · \ml{കീ} = kī · \ml{കു} = ku · \ml{കൂ} = kū · \ml{കെ} = ke · \ml{കേ} = kē · \ml{കൊ} = ko · \ml{കോ} = kō. The signs themselves are \textbf{\ml{ാ}} ā · \textbf{\ml{ി}} i · \textbf{\ml{ീ}} ī · \textbf{\ml{ു}} u · \textbf{\ml{ൂ}} ū · \textbf{\ml{െ}} e · \textbf{\ml{േ}} ē · \textbf{\ml{ൊ}} o · \textbf{\ml{ോ}} ō. (The \emph{e/o} signs are written \emph{before} their consonant but read after.)
  \item \textbf{The \emph{chandrakkala} (\ml{്}) strips the built-in vowel, and bare consonants join as conjuncts.} \ml{സ്} + \ml{ക} $\to$ \ml{സ്ക} (ska), \ml{ന്} + \ml{ദ} $\to$ \ml{ന്ദ} (nda), \ml{ല്} + \ml{ല} $\to$ \ml{ല്ല} (lla). A circle \textbf{anusvāram} (\ml{ം}) adds a final nasal.
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Independent vowels (word-initial)}

\textbf{\ml{അ}} a · \textbf{\ml{ആ}} ā · \textbf{\ml{ഇ}} i · \textbf{\ml{ഈ}} ī · \textbf{\ml{ഉ}} u · \textbf{\ml{ഊ}} ū · \textbf{\ml{എ}} e · \textbf{\ml{ഏ}} ē · \textbf{\ml{ഐ}} ai · \textbf{\ml{ഒ}} o · \textbf{\ml{ഓ}} ō · \textbf{\ml{ഔ}} au.

\section*{Worth flagging}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{The largest Dravidian alphabet.} Because Malayalam borrowed so heavily from Sanskrit, it keeps the full Sanskrit inventory — aspirates (\ml{ഖ} kh, \ml{ധ} dh…) and all three sibilants (\ml{ശ} ś, \ml{ഷ} ṣ, \ml{സ} s) — alongside the native Dravidian retroflex letters Tamil also has (\ml{ള} ḷ, \ml{ഴ} ḻ, \ml{ണ} ṇ).
  \item \textbf{Rounded forms, many conjuncts.} Malayalam's curved letters and rich stock of stacked/ligated conjuncts give it a dense, distinctive look.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Malayalam in the Dravidian family}

\textbf{Dravidian} is a family entirely separate from Indo-European (English, Latin, Sanskrit). Malayalam is the \textbf{closest sister of Tamil} — the two split from one language only about a thousand years ago — so its everyday core is strikingly Tamil-like (\emph{nandi} = Tamil \emph{naṉṟi}; \emph{illa} = \emph{illai}; \emph{śari} = \emph{sari}; the \emph{pōyi varām} farewell $\approx$ \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}). At the same time it absorbed a vast Sanskrit layer, which is why its formal greeting (\emph{namaskāram}) and its full letter-set are Sanskritised. The lessons trace, word by word, what is inherited Dravidian and what is borrowed.
